title: Shifting Baselines, Non‐Native Species and the Value of a Remote Northern Lake in New York, Northeastern United States of America
content:
ABSTRACT

Anthropogenic alterations to biological communities can cause major changes to community composition, functioning and ecosystem service provisioning; however, when these changes occur over long periods of time, they can go unnoticed due to the shifting baseline syndrome. To examine the ways shifting baselines influence the provisioning of ecosystem services, we first conducted biological surveys in Cranberry Lake, New York, a mountainous lake that has had multiple predatory fish species introduced from lowland regions of the state since the early 20th century, and compared these results to historical records on the lake's fish community. We then interviewed summer recreational lake users to determine their perceptions of the lake's biological community and what ecosystem services it provides. The biological surveys reveal a shift from the 1930s to 2020s to a fish community dominated by larger, nonnative species with more defensive structures. Many native species present in historical surveys were either entirely absent from our survey or were only found in tributary streams and not the lake itself. Our interview data showed shifted baselines related to perceptions of introduced species, a consistent strong sense of place and discussion of the support that the lake provides to the local economy. Although less disturbed lakes with high biodiversity are often conservation priorities, Cranberry Lake demonstrates that sites with reduced native species richness still can provide important ecosystem services to local communities.
